## Two ways to fail on new data

Every fitted model can report its error on the data it was fitted to. That number comes
free, and it is easy to read as a measure of how good the model is. It is not: a model
that fits its own stations perfectly can do worst of all on new sites. This page shows
why, and names the two ways a model fails on new data: too rigid to follow the pattern,
or so flexible that it follows the noise as well. The two failures need opposite fixes,
and the model's two errors, side by side, tell you which one you have.

[k-nearest neighbours](../03-supervised-learning/nearest-neighbours.qmd) met overfitting
with a single neighbour, and [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd)
watched the error on validation sites fall and then rise as a tree grew deeper. This page
names the two ends of that curve.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## Training error and the error on new data

The **training error** is a model's error on the examples it was fitted to. The error on
new data is its error on examples it has never seen, and it is the one that matters: a
model is fitted to be used on new data.

Data hold a pattern that will appear again in new data, such as warmer water holding more
of a species, and [noise](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd#averaging-the-misses-gives-the-objective)
that will not: a lucky haul, a sensor reading slightly off. A model cannot tell the two
apart, and fitting noise lowers the training error just as fitting the pattern does. Only
the pattern carries over to new data.

So the training error is usually lower than the error on new data. A rigid model, such as
a straight line, has little room to fit noise, so its two errors stay close. A flexible
model can bend through every training example, so its training error can fall to zero
while its error on new data does not. More data narrows the gap, since noise spread over
many examples is harder to fit than noise in a few.

## Underfitting and overfitting sit at the two ends of a U-shaped curve

Before it sees any data, a model is limited to a family of shapes. A straight line can only
be a straight line; a tree with four leaves can only give four different predictions. How
wide that family is, is the model's **flexibility**, also called its complexity.

- **Underfitting** is a model too rigid to follow the pattern. It misses the training data
  and new data by about as much, so its two errors are both high and close together. It is
  not fooled by noise; it simply cannot bend enough.
- **Overfitting** is a model flexible enough to follow the noise as well as the pattern. Its
  training error is low and its error on new data high, and the wide gap between them is
  the sign.

As flexibility grows, the training error keeps falling. The error on new data falls while
the model is still picking up the pattern, reaches a lowest point, then rises as the model
fits more and more noise. Plotted against flexibility, it makes a U, called the
**U-shaped error curve**. The best setting lies at its lowest point, between the two
failures, and only the error on new data shows where.

::: {.diagram}
![An underfitted model is too rigid to follow the pattern, so both its errors are high and close together. An overfitted model bends through every point, so its training error is low but its error on new data is high. The training error falls all the way; the error on new data has a lowest point in between.](img/underfitting-and-overfitting.svg){fig-alt="Three small panels show the same eleven points with a hump-shaped pattern. Too rigid, underfitting: a straight line that misses the hump. In between: a smooth curve that follows the hump. Too flexible, overfitting: a zigzag through every point. Below, a wide panel plots two errors against flexibility. The training error falls steadily to zero. The error on new data falls a little, reaches its lowest point, then rises. On the left, the underfitting zone, both errors are high and close together. On the right, the overfitting zone, the training error is low and the error on new data high, with a wide gap between them."}
:::

Both failures show up as a model that predicts badly, so they are easily confused, yet the
fixes go in opposite directions. An underfitted model needs more flexibility or better
inputs. An overfitted one needs less flexibility or more data, and
[Regularisation](regularisation.qmd) offers a third way to hold it back.

## Worked example

The data and the split by site are those of [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd):
three quarters of the monitoring sites for training and a quarter held back as test sites.
This page uses only the training sites; the test sites are kept for the end of the
section.

Each model is fitted to some of the training sites and scored on the rest, which play the
part of new sites. One such split leaves only a few dozen sites to score on, and by chance
they can be easier or harder to predict than the others. So the training sites are split
20 times at random, by site, and each error is averaged over the 20 splits.

### Preparing the data

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75)
train <- training(split)

# 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites
splits <- group_mc_cv(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75, times = 20)

predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 +
  salinity_psu + substrate + season

tree_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors())
boost_recipe <- tree_recipe |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

# A tree that stops splitting at a depth, or when a node holds fewer than
# min_n stations. The default depth is high, so that min_n alone sets its size.
tree_model <- function(min_n, depth = 30) {
  decision_tree(mode = "regression", tree_depth = depth, min_n = min_n,
                cost_complexity = 0)
}
leaves_of <- function(fitted) sum(extract_fit_engine(fitted)$frame$var == "<leaf>")

c(training_sites = n_distinct(train$site_id), splits = nrow(splits))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()

numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]
categorical = ["substrate", "season"]
predictors = numeric + categorical

grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123)
train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"]))
train = survey.iloc[train_rows]

# scikit-learn's models need numbers, so one recipe serves them all.
tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric),
    ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical),
])

# 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites
splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=20, train_size=0.75, random_state=123)
splits = list(splitter.split(train, groups=train["site_id"]))

# rpart also keeps every leaf at a third of min_n or more; this matches it.
def tree_model(min_n, depth=None):
    return DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, min_samples_split=min_n,
                                 min_samples_leaf=max(1, round(min_n / 3)),
                                 random_state=123)

{"training_sites": train["site_id"].nunique(), "splits": len(splits)}
```

:::

### The best fits to their own stations do worst on new sites

Five models from [Supervised learning](../03-supervised-learning/index.qmd) run from rigid
to flexible: linear regression; a decision tree three questions deep; a decision tree grown
out until each leaf holds a single station; a random forest of 500 trees; and boosting with
500 trees, each six questions deep. The boosted model is deliberately large, so that it has
room to fit the noise. Each is fitted to the fitting sites of every split and scored twice,
on the stations it was fitted to and on the new sites. Predicting the fitting stations'
average count everywhere, with no inputs at all, gives a baseline.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: five-models
forest_model <- rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 123)
boost_model <- boost_tree(mode = "regression", trees = 500,
                          tree_depth = 6, learn_rate = 0.1)

models <- list(
  "Linear regression"        = workflow(tree_recipe, linear_reg()),
  "Decision tree, depth 3"   = workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(2, depth = 3)),
  "Decision tree, grown out" = workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(2)),
  "Random forest"            = workflow(tree_recipe, forest_model),
  "Boosting"                 = workflow(boost_recipe, boost_model)
)

score_models <- function(s) {
  fitting <- analysis(s)
  new     <- assessment(s)
  imap(models, \(w, model) {
    fitted <- fit(w, fitting)
    tibble(model    = model,
           training = rmse_vec(fitting$abundance, predict(fitted, fitting)$.pred),
           new      = rmse_vec(new$abundance, predict(fitted, new)$.pred))
  }) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    add_row(model = "Predict the average", training = NA,
            new = rmse_vec(new$abundance, rep(mean(fitting$abundance), nrow(new))))
}

results <- map(splits$splits, score_models) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(across(c(training, new), mean)) |>
  mutate(gap = new - training) |>
  arrange(training)

results |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
def pipeline(model):
    return Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", model)])

models = {
    "Linear regression": lambda: pipeline(LinearRegression()),
    "Decision tree, depth 3": lambda: pipeline(tree_model(2, depth=3)),
    "Decision tree, grown out": lambda: pipeline(tree_model(2)),
    "Random forest": lambda: pipeline(RandomForestRegressor(
        n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5,
        random_state=123)),
    "Boosting": lambda: pipeline(GradientBoostingRegressor(
        n_estimators=500, max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.1, random_state=123)),
}

rmse = root_mean_squared_error
rows = []
for fit_rows, new_rows in splits:
    fitting, new = train.iloc[fit_rows], train.iloc[new_rows]
    for name, make in models.items():
        fitted = make().fit(fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"])
        rows.append({
            "model": name,
            "training": rmse(fitting["abundance"],
                             fitted.predict(fitting[predictors])),
            "new": rmse(new["abundance"], fitted.predict(new[predictors])),
        })
    rows.append({"model": "Predict the average", "training": np.nan,
                 "new": rmse(new["abundance"],
                             np.full(len(new), fitting["abundance"].mean()))})

results = (pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby("model", as_index=False).mean()
           .assign(gap=lambda d: d["new"] - d["training"])
           .sort_values("training", na_position="last")
           .reset_index(drop=True))

results.round(2)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: scores
#| include: false
at <- function(m, column = "new") results[[column]][results$model == m]
baseline_five <- at("Predict the average")
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-crossing
#| fig-cap: "Each model's RMSE on the stations it was fitted to and on new sites, averaged over 20 splits of the training sites. Every line rises, but by very different amounts, so the order changes. The dashed line is the error of predicting the fitting stations' average count."
#| fig-alt: "A slope chart with two positions, training on the left and new sites on the right, and RMSE on the vertical axis. Five lines join each model's training error to its error on new sites. The grown-out tree and boosting start at zero and rise steeply; the grown-out tree ends highest of all. The random forest starts at about 2 and rises to the lowest point on the right. The depth-3 tree and linear regression start highest, about 4 to 4.5, and rise gently. A dashed line marks predicting the average, about 5."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.8
results |>
  filter(model != "Predict the average") |>
  pivot_longer(c(training, new), names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |>
  mutate(set = factor(set, levels = c("training", "new"),
                      labels = c("Fitting stations", "New sites"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(set, rmse, group = model, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baseline_five, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = baseline_five + 0.25, label = "predict the average",
           colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], size = 3.4) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "RMSE (individuals)", colour = NULL,
       title = "The order on new sites is not the order on the fitting stations")
```

:::

By training error, the grown-out tree comes first with an RMSE of
`r if (at("Decision tree, grown out", "training") < 0.005) "exactly zero" else f2(at("Decision tree, grown out", "training"))`,
and boosting second at `r f2(at("Boosting", "training"))`: both have fitted their
stations almost perfectly. On new sites the order turns over. The grown-out tree comes
last, at `r f2(at("Decision tree, grown out"))`, worse than the `r f2(baseline_five)` from
predicting the average with no inputs at all, and boosting, at `r f2(at("Boosting"))`,
does no better than that average. Linear regression, last by training error, is close to
the best on new sites at `r f2(at("Linear regression"))`, behind only the random forest
at `r f2(at("Random forest"))`.

A tree with one station in each leaf predicts every fitting station as that station's own
count, so its training error is zero. It has stored the data rather than learned a
relationship from it, and the stored counts are mostly noise.

### Node size sets how closely a tree follows temperature

The setting varied in the rest of the example is a tree's **minimum node size**, `min_n`:
the smallest group of stations the tree may split into two.
[Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd) varied the depth instead.
Set large, it lets the tree split only a few times; set to 2, it lets the tree go on
splitting until each leaf holds a single station. To see what it does, three trees are
fitted to all the training stations with temperature as their only input, so that each
tree's predictions can be drawn as a line.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: one-input
temperature_recipe <- recipe(abundance ~ temperature_c, data = train) |>
  step_impute_median(temperature_c)

three_sizes <- c(300, 50, 2)
one_input <- map(three_sizes, \(n) {
  workflow(temperature_recipe, tree_model(n)) |> fit(train)
})

tibble(min_n = three_sizes, leaves = map_int(one_input, leaves_of))
```

## Python

```{python}
one_input = {
    n: Pipeline([("recipe", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                 ("model", tree_model(n))])
       .fit(train[["temperature_c"]], train["abundance"])
    for n in [300, 50, 2]
}

pd.DataFrame({"min_n": list(one_input),
              "leaves": [m["model"].get_n_leaves() for m in one_input.values()]})
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: one-input-numbers
#| include: false
one_leaves <- map_int(one_input, leaves_of)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-one-input
#| fig-cap: "Three trees fitted to the training stations with temperature as their only input. A node must hold at least 300, 50 or 2 stations before it may split. The grey points are the stations."
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("Three panels of abundance against temperature, each with grey points for the training stations and an orange step line for one tree's predictions. Left, a node needs 300 stations to split and the tree has {one_leaves[1]} leaves, so the line has a few broad, level steps. Centre, 50 stations and {one_leaves[2]} leaves, a staircase with more steps that rises and falls across the temperature range. Right, 2 stations and {one_leaves[3]} leaves, a dense comb of narrow spikes reaching up to the highest catches.")
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
grid <- tibble(temperature_c = seq(min(train$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   max(train$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   length.out = 1500))

lines <- map2(one_input, three_sizes, \(fitted, n) {
  grid |> mutate(.pred = predict(fitted, grid)$.pred, min_n = n)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

labeller <- \(n) paste0("A node needs ", n, " stations\n",
                        one_leaves[match(as.numeric(n), three_sizes)], " leaves")

ggplot(train, aes(temperature_c, abundance)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  geom_step(data = lines, aes(y = .pred), colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]],
            linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(min_n, levels = three_sizes),
             labeller = as_labeller(labeller)) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Abundance")
```

:::

The first tree has `r one_leaves[1]` leaves and gives the same prediction across wide bands
of temperature: it can show only the coarsest rise and fall. The second, with
`r one_leaves[2]` leaves, follows more of the pattern. The third has `r one_leaves[3]` leaves
and jumps up to meet nearly every large catch. Those catches are mostly luck, and a new
station at the same temperature is unlikely to repeat them.

### Sweeping the node size draws the U-shaped curve

Now the trees use all six inputs, as in [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd).
For each split, trees with 12 minimum node sizes, from 300 down to 2, are fitted to the
fitting sites and scored on the fitting stations and on the new sites.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: sweep
sizes <- c(300, 200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2)

score_sizes <- function(s) {
  fitting <- analysis(s)
  new     <- assessment(s)
  map(sizes, \(n) {
    fitted <- workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(n)) |> fit(fitting)
    tibble(min_n    = n,
           leaves   = leaves_of(fitted),
           training = rmse_vec(fitting$abundance, predict(fitted, fitting)$.pred),
           average  = rmse_vec(new$abundance, rep(mean(fitting$abundance), nrow(new))),
           new      = rmse_vec(new$abundance, predict(fitted, new)$.pred))
  }) |>
    list_rbind()
}

sweep <- map(splits$splits, score_sizes) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  group_by(min_n) |>
  summarise(across(c(leaves, training, average, new), mean)) |>
  mutate(gap = new - training) |>
  arrange(desc(min_n))

sweep |> select(-average) |> mutate(across(-min_n, \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
sizes = [300, 200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2]

rows = []
for fit_rows, new_rows in splits:
    fitting, new = train.iloc[fit_rows], train.iloc[new_rows]
    for n in sizes:
        fitted = pipeline(tree_model(n)).fit(fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"])
        rows.append({
            "min_n": n,
            "leaves": fitted["model"].get_n_leaves(),
            "training": rmse(fitting["abundance"],
                             fitted.predict(fitting[predictors])),
            "average": rmse(new["abundance"],
                            np.full(len(new), fitting["abundance"].mean())),
            "new": rmse(new["abundance"], fitted.predict(new[predictors])),
        })

sweep = (pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby("min_n", as_index=False).mean()
         .assign(gap=lambda d: d["new"] - d["training"])
         .sort_values("min_n", ascending=False)
         .reset_index(drop=True))

sweep.drop(columns="average").round(2)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: sweep-numbers
#| include: false
row_at <- function(n) filter(sweep, min_n == n)
baseline <- mean(sweep$average)
best <- slice_min(sweep, new)
stiff <- row_at(max(sizes))
# a tree that never splits predicts the average: the baseline
loose <- row_at(min(sizes))
# the most flexible tree that still beats predicting the average
last_good <- sweep |> filter(new < baseline) |> slice_max(leaves)
first_bad <- sweep |> filter(leaves > last_good$leaves) |> slice_min(leaves)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-sweep
#| fig-cap: "RMSE on the fitting stations and on new sites against the number of leaves in the tree, averaged over 20 splits of the training sites. The dashed line is the error of predicting the fitting stations' average count; the dotted line marks the lowest error on new sites."
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("Two lines of RMSE against the number of leaves on a logarithmic axis from 1 to about {round(loose$leaves)}. The training line starts at {f2(stiff$training)} with about {round(stiff$leaves)} leaves and falls ever faster to zero at the right. The line for new sites starts at {f2(stiff$new)}, dips to its lowest point, {f2(best$new)}, at about {round(best$leaves)} leaves, marked by a dotted line, then climbs to {f2(loose$new)}. A dashed line at {f2(baseline)} marks predicting the average; the line for new sites crosses above it between {round(last_good$leaves)} and {round(first_bad$leaves)} leaves.")
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
sweep |>
  pivot_longer(c(training, new), names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |>
  mutate(set = factor(set, levels = c("training", "new"),
                      labels = c("Fitting stations", "New sites"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(leaves, rmse, colour = set)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baseline, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best$leaves, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = baseline + 0.3, label = "predict the average",
           hjust = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], size = 3.4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Leaves in the tree (log scale)", y = "RMSE (individuals)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Training error falls all the way; the error on new sites does not")
```

:::

### The lowest point lies between underfitting and overfitting

**The rigid end.** With a node size of `r max(sizes)`, the largest here, the tree has
about `r round(stiff$leaves)` leaves. Its training error is `r f2(stiff$training)` and its
error on new sites `r f2(stiff$new)`, within `r f2(abs(stiff$gap))` of each other. That is
the sign of underfitting: both errors high and close together.

**The lowest point.** The error on new sites is lowest, at `r f2(best$new)`, for a node size
of `r best$min_n`, which gives trees of about `r round(best$leaves)` leaves. That beats
predicting the average, but only by `r f2(baseline - best$new)`: the counts are noisy, and
even the best tree leaves most of their variation unexplained.
[The bias–variance trade-off](bias-variance.qmd) shows why.

**The flexible end.** With a node size of 2, the tree has about `r round(loose$leaves)`
leaves and a training error of
`r if (loose$training < 0.005) "zero" else f2(loose$training)`. Its error on new sites is
`r f2(loose$new)`, worse than predicting the average. The training error gives no sign of
that: it falls smoothly all the way.

The best node size here was found by averaging over 20 splits of the training sites.
[Hyperparameter selection](hyperparameter-selection.qmd) turns that idea into the standard
method, cross-validation.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- A perfect fit is a warning sign. The **training error** is a model's error on the data
  it was fitted to, and fitting noise lowers it as much as fitting the pattern does. The
  tree that fitted every station did worse on new sites than predicting the average.
- A model's **flexibility** is how wide a family of shapes it can take. Too little and it
  **underfits**: both errors are high and close together. Too much and it **overfits**: a
  low training error and a much higher error on new data. The error on new data traces
  the **U-shaped error curve**, and its lowest point, in between, is the target.
- The fixes are opposite: more flexibility or better inputs for underfitting; less
  flexibility, regularisation or more data for overfitting.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Sweep the depth instead, as [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd)
   did. In the sweep, write `tree_model(2, depth = n)` in place of `tree_model(n)`, then set
   `sizes <- 1:15`. Averaged over 20 splits, is the lowest point at the same depth that one
   validation split chose on Decision trees?
2. Give each split fewer fitting sites by adding
   `fitting <- fitting |> filter(site_id %in% sample(unique(site_id), 30))` after the line
